topic: Why LLMs hallucinate, and how RAG helps
one_line_definition: An AI hallucination is when a chatbot confidently states something false or made up; RAG reduces this by having the AI look up trusted documents first and answer from them.
why_it_matters: People trust confident answers. Hallucinations have led to fake legal citations in court, and RAG is one of the main practical ways companies make chatbots more reliable and checkable.
pain_point: You ask a chatbot a question and it gives a fluent, confident answer, sometimes with sources, that turns out to be invented.
how_it_works: An LLM writes by predicting the next most likely word from patterns in its training data.
It optimizes for what sounds plausible, not for what is true, and has no built-in fact check.
Training and tests that reward accuracy alone encourage guessing over saying 'I don't know'.
RAG first searches a trusted knowledge source for passages relevant to the question.
Those passages are added to the prompt, so the model answers from real text and can cite it.

key_facts.fact: Hallucinations are instances where a model confidently generates an answer that isn't true.
OpenAI researchers argue language models hallucinate because standard training and evaluation procedures reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty.
If a model guesses a birthday it doesn't know, it has a 1-in-365 chance of being right, while 'I don't know' scores zero, so guessing looks better on accuracy scoreboards.
Generative AI predicts the next token from previous context; it optimizes for plausibility within the pattern, not correctness about the world, and does not 'know' what is true.
Flawed or incomplete training data and lack of grounding can cause plausible but factually incorrect outputs, even fabricated links to web pages that never existed.
RAG connects AI models with curated knowledge bases and has them source answers from that trusted content, often with citations.
A 2021 study found retrieval-augmented chatbots substantially reduce knowledge hallucination, verified by human evaluations.
RAG reduces, but does not eliminate, the chance of hallucination.
In Mata v. Avianca (2023), a US federal court fined lawyers $5,000 for submitting fake case citations generated by ChatGPT.

analogies: A student guessing on a multiple-choice exam because a blank answer scores zero (OpenAI's analogy).
Autocomplete that sounds right but never checks facts.
An open-book exam: RAG lets the AI look up the answer instead of answering from memory.
misconceptions: Hallucinations are not the AI lying on purpose; it is producing plausible text without a truth check.
RAG does not eliminate hallucinations; answers are only as good as the retrieved sources.
acronym_expansion: LLM = large language model; RAG = Retrieval-Augmented Generation
